steps.title: Load-test a prediction endpoint against tail-latency and sustainable-throughput objectives

blocks.text: Measure a capacity envelope from client outcomes, tail latency, completed work and backlog at each declared load.
Exercise the endpoint with the declared arrival/concurrency profile and bounded duration, and record client-visible outcomes and response times rather than only attempted request count.
Treat a load point as acceptable only if it meets the predeclared client-visible success and tail-latency requirements, as well as the required completed throughput.
Retain failures and timeouts separately so latency measured only for completed responses is not misrepresented as the experience of every attempted request.
Estimate client-visible success probability as successful eligible attempts divided by all eligible attempts in the defined measurement window, counting failed attempts in the denominator.
Compute the declared tail-latency percentile with np.percentile(completed_latency_values, declared_percentile), retaining its convention, sample count and time unit.
Measure successful throughput as completed successful requests divided by elapsed measurement time, and compare it with the offered load rather than equating arrivals with completed work.

blocks.caption: Authored offline attempts include multiple experiment settings. Select the declared valid-traffic load population before calculating capacity; retain errors and timeouts.
Authored unfinished-work observations for the same fixed load settings; inspect change across the measurement window.

blocks.text: Run valid and malformed HTTP JSON fixtures with assertions, keeping intentional malformed tests outside the valid-traffic capacity measurement.
At every fixed offered load, use the stated valid payload mix, warm-up and fixed measurement duration, counting successful completions, HTTP errors, timeouts and other failed attempts separately.
Compute failed-request fraction from all failed attempts divided by all valid-traffic attempts; timeouts remain failures.

Inspect backlog growth and unfinished work throughout the window; accept only stable-backlog loads meeting the predeclared tail-latency and error limits, and report the highest measured successful throughput or no feasible measured envelope.
Use docker run --name NAME -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT --env KEY=VALUE IMAGE to start the referenced image with the declared port and nonsecret runtime settings.

Serialize structured request/response values with json.dumps; decode JSON with json.loads before inspecting fields.
Use np.mean(numeric_values) for the arithmetic mean of the selected numeric observations.
Use np.std(numeric_values, ddof=0): divide squared deviations by N, then take the square root. Use ddof=1 only when the declared calculation requires N−1.
Assert the declared valid, boundary and failure predicates. In ordinary non-optimized execution, a false assertion raises AssertionError.

steps.title: Compare completed throughput with backlog

blocks.text: Inspect the registered valid-traffic attempts alongside unfinished work. Keep HTTP errors, timeouts and other failures separate, but include all valid attempts in success and failed-fraction denominators. Calculate successful completions per measurement time, not arrivals per time. Percentiles describe completed-response samples with declared units and convention, not timed-out responses. Accept only stable-backlog points meeting all declared latency, error and throughput objectives, or report no feasible measured envelope. Intentional malformed fixtures stay outside this capacity population.
Arrivals are not completed work. A low latency for completed responses cannot hide timeouts, and a growing backlog is not a stable acceptable load point.

Select only tested load points satisfying every predeclared probability, error, p99, throughput and backlog requirement. Report the highest measured successful throughput among those passing points, or explicitly report ‘no feasible measured envelope’ if none pass; make no unmeasured production-capacity claim.

Demand/capacity verdict
```
At the same declared offered load, use all eligible attempts for success probability, all completed successful latencies for p99 (linear, seconds, count stated), completed successes / measurement seconds for throughput, np.mean and np.std(ddof=0). Safe YAML round trip and resolved fields preserve approved immutable image and runtime settings. More-is-always-better trap
```
```
Choose the largest supplied replica count without regard to its measured timeout fraction, absent successful latency sample and unfinished-request evidence. More replicas alone prove it meets every objective.
```

No restoration

```
Changed replica and instance settings remain active after the bounded check; report calls written YAML a restoration without inspecting restored runtime state.
```

steps.title: Carry these rules forward

blocks.text: Arrivals are not completions; timeouts and growing backlog cannot be hidden by low completed-response latency.
Include batch waiting in full request latency; fast execution alone does not meet the objective.
Configuration is intent. Compare observed workers and same-interval resource evidence with the declared bound.
More replicas are not guaranteed to pass; distinguish intended counts, observed counts and completed throughput.

blocks.text: Exercise the endpoint with the declared arrival/concurrency profile and bounded duration, and record client-visible outcomes and response times rather than only attempted request count.

remediation_steps.title: Try again: Load-test a prediction endpoint against tail-latency and sustainable-throughput objectives

blocks.text: Exercise the endpoint with the declared arrival/concurrency profile and bounded duration, and record client-visible outcomes and response times rather than only attempted request count.

Inspect backlog growth and unfinished work throughout the window; accept only stable-backlog loads meeting the predeclared tail-latency and error limits, and report the highest measured successful throughput or no feasible measured envelope.
Treat a load point as acceptable only if it meets the predeclared client-visible success and tail-latency requirements, as well as the required completed throughput.
Retain failures and timeouts separately so latency measured only for completed responses is not misrepresented as the experience of every attempted request.
Estimate client-visible success probability as successful eligible attempts divided by all eligible attempts in the defined measurement window, counting failed attempts in the denominator.
Compute the declared tail-latency percentile with np.percentile(completed_latency_values, declared_percentile), retaining its convention, sample count and time unit.
Measure successful throughput as completed successful requests divided by elapsed measurement time, and compare it with the offered load rather than equating arrivals with completed work.
At every fixed offered load, use the stated valid payload mix, warm-up and fixed measurement duration, counting successful completions, HTTP errors, timeouts and other failed attempts separately.
Compute failed-request fraction from all failed attempts divided by all valid-traffic attempts; timeouts remain failures.
Arrivals are not completed work. A low latency for completed responses cannot hide timeouts, and a growing backlog is not a stable acceptable load point.

remediation_steps.title: Try again: Choose inference batching under latency constraints

blocks.text: Match each successful JSON response to its request identity and batching setting before computing its end-to-end duration from the trace.
Use response-completion minus request-start time in one declared unit, including batch waiting time in the latency interpretation.
Calculate the required tail percentile with np.percentile(latencies, declared_percentile), keeping the convention and successful-response sample count explicit.
Choose only a batching limit meeting the stated latency objective, comparing the same trace/population interpretation.
Batch waiting belongs in the stated end-to-end latency. A faster execution interval alone does not make a batching limit acceptable under the full request objective.

remediation_steps.title: Try again: Configure bounded prediction-worker concurrency on an existing runtime

blocks.text: A Compose YAML document declares services by name; use indented mappings for service fields and lists or mappings in the forms required by the Compose specification.
Set a service’s image to its immutable artifact reference, its ports to HOST:CONTAINER mappings, and its environment to the declared nonsecret key/value settings.
Use docker compose -f CONFIG_PATH config to parse, resolve and validate the authored YAML before applying it; check its resolved fields against the intended runtime contract.
Set the existing runtime’s worker-limit setting in the YAML, validate its parsed value and run the referenced image under that bound.
Inspect running worker processes with docker container top NAME during the load fixture and compare the observed count with the configured limit to detect oversubscription.
Inspect concurrent CPU/memory usage during the same fixture to support the bound check rather than assuming the configuration was honored.

With the declared PyYAML dependency, import yaml; write a mapping/list configuration with yaml.safe_dump(config, file_handle), reload it with yaml.safe_load(file_handle), and inspect the required resolved fields before submitting it to the existing runtime. Safe loading supports standard YAML tags, not arbitrary Python object constructors.

blocks.text: Restore the nonproduction runtime’s original replica and lifecycle settings after the bounded scaling check.

blocks.text: For a fixed Compose scaling fixture, declare deploy.replicas or use docker compose up -d --scale SERVICE=COUNT, then inspect the actual replica count.

Use np.std(numeric_values, ddof=0): divide squared deviations by N, then take the square root. Use ddof=1 only when the declared calculation requires N−1.
